messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sokha is a 66-year-old Cambodian American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a roofer, a trade he had always taken pride in for its physical demands and the steadiness it gave his family. He is married, and before the incident he thought of himself as dependable, the kind of man who could keep going through heat, height, and long days without complaint. The event that now returns to him happened on a roofing job when he was exposed to toxic chemicals. He remembers the scene with an unusual sharpness: the smell hitting first, harsh and synthetic, the kind of industrial odor that seemed to coat the inside of his nose and throat; the confusion on the roof as he realized something was wrong; the sense that he could not trust his own body to tell him what would happen next. Even now, the memory comes back with the clarity of a film, replaying in sequence with details he does not want but cannot seem to blur.

In the weeks afterward, what unsettled Sokha was not only that he could remember the exposure so vividly, but that at other times the feeling of that moment would come over him with no picture attached. He could be sitting at home and suddenly feel the same dread and alarm in his body, as if the danger were present again, without any clear image of the roof or the chemicals. He tried hard not to think about what had happened. If the memory began to form, he would push it away, tell himself to stop, get up and busy himself with something else. But the effort left him tense and worn out. At night, waking in the dark was especially difficult. In those first seconds before orienting himself, he would feel exposed and unsafe, his body already braced. Darkness itself became charged for him. Nighttime no longer felt like ordinary rest; it felt like vulnerability.

Certain smells became almost impossible to tolerate. Antiseptic odors, the smell of hospitals, and other related chemical smells could pull him back immediately. The link made sense to him because scent had been so central to the original exposure. When he encountered those odors now, it was as though his mind and body recognized danger before he had time to think. Even routine situations became complicated. If he had to enter a medical building, he would notice the disinfectant smell right away and feel himself tighten. On job sites, if there were unfamiliar materials or strong odors, he became preoccupied and distracted, scanning and second-guessing.

Over time Sokha came to believe that the world was a dangerous place in a way he had not fully understood before. He was no longer confident in his own judgment. What troubled him most was the feeling that he could not rely on himself: if he had missed the danger once, how could he trust himself now? He found it difficult to relax even in places he knew were safe. His attention was often divided, and he had more trouble concentrating, something that was especially unsettling in roofing work, where focus matters. He also became reluctant to go to unfamiliar places because he felt he could not assess what danger might be there. If his wife suggested going somewhere new, he preferred to stay home or let her go with someone else. The habit narrowed their life together.

At work and at home, Sokha also became markedly less willing to disagree with anyone. He kept quiet, went along, and avoided asserting himself because conflict felt like one more thing he could not manage. This had practical consequences. On roofing crews, where men often have to speak up quickly and clearly, he held back rather than question plans or raise concerns. At home, his wife noticed that he no longer spoke with the same certainty about ordinary decisions. He spent a great deal of time dwelling on how he used to be before the exposure—stronger, clearer, more sure of himself. Those comparisons were painful. He had begun to think in bleak terms about the future, as if there were no real future left for him beyond enduring day to day with less confidence and less freedom.

By the time he sought help, Sokha was tired of living in constant readiness. What finally brought him in was the accumulation of small moments: waking in the dark with his heart already clenched, losing focus on jobs, feeling overcome by a smell in a place other people found ordinary, and seeing how much of his life had shrunk around avoiding what felt unsafe. He is frightened that this is now simply who he is, a man who cannot trust himself in a dangerous world. At the same time, he is hoping, quietly but seriously, that treatment might help him feel steady enough to sleep through the night, go where he needs to go, and stop measuring himself only against the man he believes he used to be.
